abstract.para: Because the journal stores data in a binary format, you cannot open it directly with tools such as cat or less. Use the journalctl command to query and display its content instead.

topic.para: Called without any options, journalctl shows all logged messages, oldest first, piped through a pager:

tip.title: Matching by executable
tip.para: Besides options, journalctl also accepts a bare executable path as a match, showing only messages from that executable.

topic.para: The following options cover the most common queries:

listitem.para: Shows only the most recent journal messages, and prints new log entries as they are added to the journal.
Prints the messages and jumps to the end of the journal, so that the latest entries are visible within the pager.
Prints the messages of the journal in reverse order, so that the latest entries are listed first.
Shows only kernel messages. This is equivalent to the field match _TRANSPORT=kernel.
Shows only messages for the specified &systemd; unit. This is equivalent to the field match _SYSTEMD_UNIT=UNIT.

example.title: Viewing messages from a single service
example.screen: Sep 07 09:23:59 sles16 sshd-session[4782]: Accepted publickey for tux from 192.168.122.1 port 57432 ssh2 Sep 07 09:23:59 sles16 sshd-session[4782]: pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user tux(uid=1000) by tux(uid=0)

listitem.para: Shows messages from the current boot, or, with a negative offset, from an earlier one. For example, -b -1 shows the previous boot.
Shows only messages at the given priority level or more severe (so -p err shows err, crit, alert, and emerg, but not warning or anything less severe). See for what the priority levels mean.
Limits the output to a time range, for example, --since today or --since "09:00" --until "10:00".

topic.para: For the complete list of options and journal field names, see man 1 journalctl and man 7 systemd.journal-fields.

important.title: logrotate does not manage the journal
important.para: logrotate only rotates the plain-text files under /var/log. The journal's own binary storage in /var/log/journal/ is unaffected by it and, unless you have set a limit in a journald.conf.d drop-in, is only capped by &systemd;'s built-in default (a percentage of the file system it resides on).

topic.para: Check the journal's current disk usage, and trim it manually if needed, with:
--vacuum-time=TIME (for example, --vacuum-time=2weeks) and --vacuum-files=COUNT work the same way, removing the oldest archived journal files until the given age or file count is reached.
